column121: During cruise flight at 3;000 ft. a traffic alert was issued by Approach Control. He stated 'Crossing traffic at 11 o'clock 1 mile; 200 ft. below you at 2;800 ft.'. He also stated unverified since he had no two way communication with the traffic he had pointed out to me. Again; he called 'traffic at 11 o'clock; 1/2 mile; 200 ft. below you at 2;800 MSL'. At this point the TCAS started alerting me to a potential collision and since we have no RA capabilities I took the evasive action of a cyclic climb until I was approx. 3;300 ft. I still did not have the crossing traffic in sight. Shortly thereafter; a small single engine Cherokee airplane flew directly underneath us. I am convinced he never saw us and since he was not talking to Approach Control he had no idea he had become a conflict for us. ATC had no way to verify if he had the correct altimeter setting and I am convinced had I not initiated a climb we would have had a potential collision at cruise speed. ATC did everything they could to warn us; and our equipment gave me another clue of a potential problem but until corrective action was taken; the conflicting traffic was not spotted until it would have been too late. Always use Approach Control and the radar service they provide even if you are not landing at their primary airport. If this crossing traffic had simply been on frequency and been radar identified; this event would never have happened. Trust your equipment and know how to interpret the data that is being presented. Since we do not have RA capability; you must determine altitude of the traffic by looking at the target displayed altitude and making a decision about a climb; turn or descent. The system will not present the solution on the VSI as a RA system will do.

column121: On departure from APA [we were] initially given runway heading. Soon after departure; tower gave [us] a clearance to turn and climb to the east along with a traffic advisory of traffic entering the downwind. TCAS showed a traffic conflict with traffic within 3 miles and 300 ft. We requested a runway heading until clear of traffic. Afterwards; tower cleared to turn east and contact TRACON. TRACON gave [us] a traffic alert with traffic within 700 ft. of our assigned Altitude. Crew requested a climb to avoid traffic converging traffic. Traffic then advised as maneuvering and shown on a TCAS within 400 ft. Last call of traffic 400 ft. below us and gave us direct fix ZZZZZ toward the previous reported trafficking. Many aircraft within airspace while multiple clearances were blocked to include our clearance to ZZZZZ. A clearance to maintain 9;000 ft. was received. At some point both crew members agreed 10;000 ft. was the altitude. A short time later we received an RA and ATC gave an immediate descent and turn to heading 360 and maintain 9;000 ft. ATC gave a phone number to call once on ground. Two close encounters within 4 minutes of takeoff with VFR traffic: one on takeoff and one before turn to ZZZZZ; both less than 500 ft. separation.Additional TRACON frequencies [are needed] during high workload times. Multiple blocked transmissions and VFR flight following request in short time on this frequency. Crew both agreed 10;000 ft. selected in the window. Potential wrong altitude set and agreed upon in altitude selector.

column121: Aircraft was cleared for the RNAV (GPS) RWY XXR at ZZZ. PF armed APP mode and commenced the approach. Passing ZZZZZ [fix]; PF was utilizing EVS (Enhanced Vision System) and HUD in an attempt to see runway lights. PF continued to focus on EVS and HUD when GROUND PROX illuminated almost the same time as a TERRAIN ALERT call from ZZZ Tower was received between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1. Aircraft was level at 1;100 feet; where it climbed to regain VPATH to continue approach. PF and PM both had vertical ground contact and were familiar with local terrain (ZZZ is aircraft's home base) and were comfortable reacquiring the VPATH and continuing approach.Suggest using EVS and HUD as secondary tool during. Verify APP has properly captured prior to shifting focus to EVS and HUD.
column123: During RNAV XXR approach to ZZZ with approach close to minimums the Tower called low altitude alert almost simultaneously with Ground Prox warning.  The approach had been setup properly and I saw the PF arm approach mode when we were cleared to switch to tower.  I went heads down to change frequency and checked in with tower.  Shortly thereafter the Tower called a low altitude alert and ground proximity called terrain.  At that time I noticed that we were well below the vertical path but I could see the ground and almost immediately the tower on my right side which we were well clear of.  I told PF to level off and even climb a couple hundred feet.  We were able to rejoin the V Path about ZZZZZ1 on the approach and continued down to MDA where we were able to proceed visually when the runway was observed visually.  If we were not at our local airport with local knowledge of the terrain I am sure I would have called for a go around.I believe that the PF was focused inside the HUD on the EVS looking for runway lights and lost his instrument scan.  As the PM I also lost situational awareness.  Really have no idea how we ended up I believe in a pitch hold mode with the autopilot and no idea how it did not capture the V Path.

column121: The aircraft had been sitting for a great length of time so it was decided the aircraft should be test flown prior to its first revenue flight. During the initial checks; the radar system failed the test cycles; so the discrepancy was noted in the logbook and maintenance was performed (approximately one hour). All other checks were satisfactory. Taxi normal. Initial takeoff normal 80-kt call normal. At approximately 110 kts I noticed my airspeed indication had blanked. Taxi was indicated in the window. I glanced to the right the FO (First Officer) indications appeared to be normal. We were rapidly approaching V1/Vr 135 kts so I elected to continue. V1/Vr was called and I rotated at a normal rate after the nose wheel left the ground my airspeed tape reappeared; however; the indication was approximately 90-100 kts with visual stall indications. No shaker. Positive rate was called and the gear was raised. At about 100 feet. I transferred control to the pilot monitoring. I had IAS comparator in the PFD and multiple levels one and two alerts. SEL Manual Feel Sel Fadec ALTN (3). A combination of those alerts drives the user to 'Refer to Emergency Non-Alert procedure- AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE.' I called to the pilot in the OBS seat to get the QRH out. I was also handling multiple radio calls. Notified ATC that we had issues with airspeed indications and erratic altimetry issues and to keep us within 20 NM of ZZZ and that we would be returning to ZZZ. The FCP was blanking on numerous occasions we were cleared to 10;000 ft however the altitude window would blank on occasion. Between 6;000-7;000 feet we were trying to ascertain what readouts were accurate as the right-side airspeed was giving erroneous indications altitude readouts seemed erroneous as well. Captain side was reading 90 kts FO side 270 knots standby 230 kts. I asked for a ground speed readout from ATC 380 kts was the response. Then as we leveled at 10;000 feet my airspeed and altitude indications returned to normal as did the FOs. We returned to ZZZ with no other issues. Blocking in Maintenance noted two ADC failures generated by the CFDS below 300 feet.

column121: Taxiing out to gate Captain had issues with his FD (Flight Director). Captain placed his FD source to #2. All appeared well. Normal takeoff until 400 ft. At 400 ft. the Captain commanded NAV proformance. I selected NAV and PROF from the GCP. Shortly afterwards the Captain asked for Autoflight. When pressing Autoflight the AP2 annuncated in the FMA. I pressed Autoflight again but AP2 remained enunciated. I mentioned this to the Captain. ATC then cleared us to fix ZZZZZ and I announced NAV Available because we were still runway heading; then noticed that Nav Armed was anticipated; but hadn't captured. The Captain used the heading select function. To keep the aircraft on the correct path. At this point we also noticed that the engines were still in Takeoff Thrust Limit. We tried several times to see if NAV would react or anything; but any FMS derived values to the GCP or autopilot did not work. As we continued climb we began to evaluate if we should continue the flight. As a team of three we double-checked all such settings and possibilities. There was no obvious action and the buttons pushed on the FMS and GCP didn't have the desired results. When the PROF key was pressed to display the climb page all values were blank or boxes. At this time we also were not sure of the reliability of our NAV function. With the degradation in our autopilot for maintaining course assigned route as we only had HDG and insecurity to the accuracy of the FMS NAV data presented to us and our route the Captain made the decision to return to the departure airport and we all were in concurrence with his decision. We then went through WAADS verifying weather at ZZZ; starting APU and starting fuel dump. During dump an ACARS message was sent to company advising of turn back. As we were dumping; ZZZ control vectored us south of ZZZ for dumping and eventual vectors Runway XX. After dump auto stopped and we turned dump off from the fuel pump switch there was a LVL 2 Dump VLV 2 Disag. The checklist was completed for this with the system in auto; a note was do not pressurize then cross feed manifolds. However we had a LVL 2 LAT FUEL UNBAL but could not follow the procedure as it requires us to pressurize the crossfeed manifold and the previous checklist was to not pressurize the manifolds. The system in Auto wasn't opening the crossfeed manifold and we chose not to. The approach was setup and briefed for ILS Runway XX and as we advised of ready for approach. On descent we noticed there were no overspeed or low speed warning bars on the airspeed indicator. As we slowed around 200 kts. in descent clean config the stick shaker turned on; power was added and airspeed increased causing the stick shaker to turn off. We then extended slats and we're vigilant about our speed since we realized we didn't have normal cues. When vectoring form the ILS the FMS was still enunciating NAV Armed. The all/land button was not responsive so the decision was to fly the approach manual as we could not determine if the autopilot was going to go on to the appropriate mode. Upon intercept of the localizer; we were right to the glideslope as well and got above the glide path and the approach became unstabilized. We executed a missed approach and advised tower. Tower asked if we were requesting priority handling; we responded negative but asked for a longer vector and ATC advised we'd get a 16 mile final and gave us a downwind vector. As the FMS was setup for a second approach the NAV Armed annunciation went blank. As we were vectored to the final; the APPR/Land enunciated normally. On localizer indication becoming active; the autopilot captured the localizer and a normal approach to landing was made. As our normal policy when a fuel dump is made emergency equipment followed us along the runway and taxiways to parking to insure that there was no hazmat leaks or FOD from the aircraft.

column121: Aircraft X was on ILS approach to Runway 4 at GSP when a VFR aircraft inbound to GMU went across final under Aircraft X. Traffic was called. GMU [Tower] was called. Aircraft X was below the clouds and stated he would execute missed approach if there was a RA. The pilot seemed to stay above glide slope to avoid the RA. Both aircraft eventually got each other in sight and Aircraft X landed.This is a known safety problem. The closest proximity of 2 aircraft in this situation is zero lateral and less than 100 feet vertical if the GSP arrival is on the glideslope and the VFR is in the GMU Delta airspace. However; it should not be taken for granted that aircraft on instrument and visual approaches will be at or above glideslope altitude. Since the VFR is under the GSP arrival; which is usually a jet; there are also wake turbulence issues.The Charlie and Delta airspace design is flawed. The FAA is either unwilling or unable to redesign the airspace to provide for the safety of the flying public.From my experience; the VFR aircraft involved are always inbound to GMU from SC72 (Chandelle). It is probably less than half a dozen aircraft that occasionally do this. When they depart GMU; they are instructed to fly over VPLOW when GSP Runway 4 is in use. If they were instructed to fly over VPLOW when inbound to GMU; the problem would be resolved. GMU Tower can instruct aircraft to remain outside the Delta and instruct aircraft where to enter the Delta; so there is no reason this solution would not work. It could be agreed to; briefed and implemented in 24 hours.This situation develops quickly and there are no guarantees that the controllers will see it before the RA or collision alert. When it is seen; or when the alarms go off; what does FAA management want the controllers to do?  Should we be breaking off the approach as a preventive measure?

column121: On a flight to LAX; after being cleared for the approach for Runway 25L around 9 DME our aircraft was snapped hard to the right due to wake turbulence from a preceding MD11. Continuous turbulence; crew climbed above glide path & a dot off of localizer to the right primarily due to the direction the wake snapped us. A B-737 was on the approach for [Runway] 25R. They were in sight the entire time. Crew corrected back on course. Crew stayed high on glide slope; at 100 ft. some turbulence was encountered. There was no wind during the entire approach.
column123: On approach (estimate 2500 ft. MSL) above clouds we encountered wake turbulence from a 'heavy' aircraft landing ahead of us. Aircraft was properly configured for landing and on profile. Wings rocked left and then right by 15 degrees or so; but rapidly. I recall that we exited the turbulence in a right bank and held a course perhaps 5 to 10 degrees right of course as we both acknowledged verbally what had happened. I called Tower and advised them we had experienced wake turbulence. ATC responded by asking our intentions and I responded that we were deviating right. ATC responded not to deviate right. Both PF (Pilot Flying) and I saw an aircraft to our right; presumably on parallel approach. We maintained visual separation from it and the PF returned to the LOC centerline; now maintaining a profile slightly higher than GS. We continued the approach and landed without further incident. Our flight up to this point had been characterized by light to moderate turbulence along the majority of our route; resulting in many altitude changes in attempt to find smoother air for our passengers. The flight itself was fatiguing.I have to admit that I was anticipating the end of the flight and was not properly considering contingencies for wake turbulence. Proper SA (Situational Awareness) would have led me to help the PF out by suggesting that he climb; or deviate left rather than right. I also think that we as a crew need to include wake turbulence in any approach briefing at airports where heavies are operating; and where parallel approaches are in progress.

column121: Descending out of FL400 with a speed restriction of Mach .76; were directed to cross PURSE at FL340. We started to descend at 1;500 fpm. Around FL370; the aircraft suddenly banked to the left about 45 degrees and we experienced some negative G's. The autopilot switched off and we put power to idle and opposite control inputs. The aircraft then banked up to 45 degrees to the right. We leveled the wings; and noted an additional 3;500 fpm descent rate while passing through FL350. We gradually increased pitch angle to get back to a 1;500 fpm descent and leveled off at FL340. All three crew members were seated with seat belts fastened. No injuries reported. However; the interior was a mess from all the food; water; glasses; magazines; that got thrown around. Immediately after the event; we reported it to ATC and queried about preceding traffic. We were told that there was an Airbus A320 eight miles ahead that was in a descent. In order to avoid any further incidents; we requested to veer off the JANNY4 arrival; and paralleled the course.

column121: Instructional flight years ago with really good instrument student in stage 3 of a Part 141 program.  Doing cross-country IFR flight planning from ZZZ to POU and student requested to do the VOR Runway 24 approach at POU.  He wanted to work on VOR navigation and using 2 OBS for a non-precision approach. I thought it was a good idea until we had some trouble with ATC that day. I don't know if date is 100% correct; but it was close to Date; which is what made me think of it this year. We requested the approach and then the Controller was very busy confusing it with the VOR-A approach into POU. After attempting to clarify; he proceeded to give us radar vectors for the approach. Both the student and I were a little confused; but went with it despite out actual attitude being less than prescribed for each quadrant of the approach plate. ATC vectoring altitudes can be lower and we were VFR in some turbulence; 10+ SM visibility and clear with no ceilings. The reason for concern was that it is a hilly area and if 'Vectored to Final'; it is directly over the path of the ZZZ1 traffic pattern. There was also some confusion over this instruction as 99% of the time when you are 'Vectored-to-final' the 'intermediate' course is identical to the 'final' approach course with respect to heading/course changes/corrections. Did he want us to fly to the intermediate segment (course 218); intercept; and then remain on segment of published approach; or did he want us to fly to intercept 242 final approach course before that and continue with vectors?  Upon looking this up in 7110 afterwards there seems to be some confusion and ambiguity with these terms when intermediate segment is not the same 'course'.  Being VFR we continued as instructed; but if it were IMC this could be extremely problematic. We were low over unfamiliar terrain; irregular topography; another airport; in turbulence; and NOT on a segment of the published approach; above minimums; until passing the VOR into final. The flight continued there and back without incident and caused the student and I to look into ATC instructions; PIC compliance; instrument approaches; and safe practices during instrument procedures during our next ground lesson. I apologize for not including this form in the lesson during our ground debrief and recap of the situation. It could have been more accurate and useful had we done it with it fresh in our minds.
